newsitem.title: CHINA: China fixes tax for foreign banks' yuan business.
newsitem.headline: China fixes tax for foreign banks' yuan business.

text.p: China announced Tuesday a preferential tax rate of 15 percent for foreign banks doing business in its local currency but limited them to dealing with foreign-funded firms registered in Shanghai.
The banks are Citibank, a unit of New York-based Citicorp, Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp., Tokyo-Mitsubishi Bank and the Industrial Bank of Japan.

Foreign bankers expressed surprise at the rate -- the same as their foreign currency business is taxed -- and much lower than the 33 percent rate for Chinese banks doing the same business with the same clients.

But bankers with local Chinese commercial banks said they were not worried about the decision, saying the scope of the local currency business that foreign banks would be allowed to conduct would be highly restrictive for years to come.
The four foreign banks were chosen by the People's Bank of China to do local currency deposit and loan business.
All foreign banks in China previously were restricted to doing business in foreign currency and most have been eager to gain a share of the huge local market for yuan deposits and loans.
The official Xinhua news agency said that about 10 foreign banks had applied to the central bank for the right to start yuan business.

According to rules issued by the central bank, foreign banks can accept yuan deposits only from foreign-funded firms or from foreign individuals or deposits from Chinese enterprises derived from the banks' loans to them.
The banks can supply yuan loans only to foreign-funded firms or Chinese enterprises that have previously obtained foreign currency loans from the banks, the rules said.
